Du hood aux planches: From the Hood to the Stage
Dans PAS FOUT’ MIND, Eric Vega raconte s: In PAS FOUT’ MIND, Eric Vega recounts his journey from the Montréal hood to the stage, a rare story about social class and identity.
José Flores, Eric Vega, Léa Noblet Di Zi:
José Flores, Eric Vega, Léa Noblet Di Ziranaldi and Kevin Jr Maddripp share their relationship to the hood and the paths that led them to the stage.

Quand je suis tombée sur l’annonce de <e: When I came across the announcement for PAS FOUT’ MIND, a play about the hood, I was surprised I hadn’t been invited. But above all, I was glad I hadn’t missed it. I immediately told Lela about it, pointing out that the subject was, precisely, very Converse.
Au-delà de cela, c’est aussi une histoir: Beyond that, it’s also a story we never see represented in theatre, where social class issues are rarely addressed – I was also surprised that I didn’t know Eric Vega’s name. Fortunately, this conversation was made possible thanks to the artists and the Quat’ Sous theatre, who managed to give us some of their time despite a busy schedule – the play is running almost to a sold-out house. I hope you’ll get the chance to see it.
« Tu penses que je peux écrire sur le <e: “Do you think I can write about the hood ?” actor Eric Vega asks right off the bat on the stage of the Quat’ Sous theatre. In PAS FOUT’ MIND, a play of his own making, the 31-year-old actor draws on his childhood, spent in the neighbourhoods of eastern Montréal in a Latin American family, and on the path that led him to a career in theatre. It’s a story that may seem atypical, but one in which many will recognize themselves.
Sans détour, il y a tout d’abord le titr: Plainly, there’s first the title, which is in slang. PAS FOUT’ MIND means “We don’t care,” says Eric Vega, who plays himself in the play. On stage, he explains to those who don’t know the language of the street what each expression refers to, bringing the audience along with him on the adventure. “A hand is extended to the audience. We thought that was really important,” explains producer Xavier Inchauspé. “People had to understand,” adds director Philippe Boutin.
En l’espace d’une heure à peine, entre d: In barely an hour, somewhere between mockery and disillusionment, Eric tells the story of his character, from a troubled childhood in the hood to a stint in the army, then, against all odds, to theatre studies.
« Je me suis rendu compte, durant le pro: “I realized, during the process, that my story isn’t only my story. It’s a pretext to put on stage a whole range of things we never see, or rarely see,” says Eric. “It’s not just my story, it’s a vehicle for these stories that aren’t only mine,” he adds.
« Il y a plein de façons de sortir du <e: “There are plenty of ways to get out of the hood ,” says Eric. “But we don’t necessarily want to get out of the hood,” he immediately corrects, underlining the ambivalence. He talks about the ways of doing it with humour in the play. “I say there are three options. Option 1 is the straight line of school. Option 2 is work – manual work: you do a vocational diploma (DEP), you become a mechanic, you work in construction. The army falls under that. And option 3: the street shits. You do crime,” says Eric.
C’est également la voie la plus dangereu: It’s also the most dangerous path. “But it’s the worst way to get out of the hood, because if you get caught, you enter a vicious circle.”
Le comédien parle à partir de sa propre: The actor speaks from his own experience. “I tried all three, that’s what the show is about. If I’d taken option 1 and humble down from the start, I would have spared myself a lot of trouble. At the same time, that’s the adventure of life,” Eric elaborates.
Toutefois, il ne se fait pas moralisateu: Still, he doesn’t moralize. “I’d say the majority of people in the hood are going to be fine,” he argues. “They’ll choose option 1; they’ll have a good life. There’s a part of the hood’s population that finds itself in other circumstances. When I was young and ran around with street gangs, causing chaos and looking for trouble, at some point I understood that there’s something called ‘intergenerational trauma,’” says Eric.
Il évoque alors l’instabilité dans laque: He then speaks of the instability in which his parents grew up. “Fear gets passed down. Maybe I was running through the streets looking for trouble because it was my instinct; that’s what was passed on to me: that we’re supposed to run everywhere. It’s hard to understand that when you’re young.”
Il se rappelle ceux qui lui ont tendu la: He remembers those who reached out a hand in those moments, notably a police officer who got him out of several situations when he was a minor. “He did good work, that officer. I was lucky to have a guy like that,” he says gratefully. “But why is he on my case?” young Eric wondered. “I was able to see signs like that, telling me that maybe I had to try to go down another path,” he continues. “Life will present signs, but you have to know how to take them. It’s up to us to take the step. But we all have a path deep inside us.”
C’est ainsi qu’à 16 ans, Eric choisit l’: And so at 16, Eric chose the army to straighten himself out. “It’s a survival state. Some are going to get caught, end up in a youth centre, not finish high school. But it’s never too late afterward.” The actor cites as an example an acquaintance from the neighbourhood, who didn’t have it easy, whom he ran into recently at the flea market. Today, this old friend is doing well: “He made it. He looked good. He found his path. He sells Interac machines. Hold on and try something. Try something different.”
Malgré tous les obstacles, Eric est pers: Despite all the obstacles, Eric is convinced he made the right career choice. “It’s like a feeling, an instinct. It’s a little voice deep inside us that tells us we have what it takes. And that’s what you have to follow. Nobody is going to understand you. Nobody. And that’s okay. Keep going, and at some point you’ll cross paths with people who understand,” he advises.
Quand le comédien n’a pas de contrat de: When the actor has no theatre or TV contract, he works in construction. “I do roofing,” he says. It’s a trade his father understands much better. “Every summer, he says: ‘Hey, start your own company, you’d be good at it.’ It’s normal, [our parents] want the best for us,” Eric illustrates.
Les rénovations et le travail artistique: Renovations and artistic work: that’s the financial balance he’s found to pursue his passion. “It’s hard. But you have to find a recipe: every artist will find the recipe that works for them,” he sums up. “I’m lucky to be good with my hands. But it’s also work and interest that I put into it,” the actor argues. “Hustle, hustle, hustle, it will never stop. When you come from the hood, what can seem like a handicap becomes your strength. A privileged kid who doesn’t know any of that can’t tell the story I’m telling on stage tonight.”
« Dans chaque chapitre, je sentais l’env: “In every chapter, I felt Eric’s desire to bring in the community. At every stage – the hood, the army, the theatre – there’s community. It’s a solo, but in this story, there are a lot of mentors around him,” notes director Philippe Boutin. “I’m 31, I’ll be looking for mentorship my whole life. I think it’s the way, letting yourself be guided, finding more experienced people and letting yourself be guided, and humble down,” Eric answers.
Il reste conscient que les choses ne son: He remains aware that things aren’t the same between the hood of his childhood and today’s. “In the play, I tell the version I lived when I was young. Things have already changed a lot,” Eric points out. “I know some people who are more connected to the reality young people live today. The game has changed. It’s even harder, more chaotic than what I knew. And more accessible.” Still, he refuses to be discouraged and sees these young people’s potential. “I was lucky, but I also knew how to see my luck. And I believe they’re all capable of seeing it.”
« Le <em>hood</em>, c’est universel », d: “The hood is universal,” says Kevin Jr Maddripp, a professional dancer who performs in PAS FOUT’ MIND. He grew up in the French banlieues. “One of my best friends said, when we were young: ‘Where you come from, yes, it’s predefined, but it’s not necessarily the end, the place where everything stops.’ If you come from a disadvantaged neighbourhood and your origins are different, it’s not necessarily a handicap, but a strength. That’s what you should take as power, as strength to destroy the stereotypes and norms people have,” he says.
Lui-même s’était tourné, alors qu’il éta: When he was younger and more studious, he himself had turned to studies in electromechanics. “When I discovered dance, I was in school; I was supposed to get my bac, start a company, like option 2. I had good grades, my mother was happy,” the dancer recounts. Then he started skipping classes to go dance. “It became an obsession.”
« J’ai appris la danse dans la rue. Ma m: “I learned dance on the street. My mother thought I was selling drugs, she was going crazy,” he says. Once the secret came out, it was still hard to win her over. “My mother absolutely didn’t want it. There was a fight at home, right up until my very first contracts,” Kevin remembers. Then she was convinced when she saw the effort he was putting in. “She told me: ‘I think this is your calling.’”
José Flores, danseur professionnel depui: José Flores, a professional dancer since 2017, knows something about that. His parents didn’t always approve of his career choice. In the Montréal hood of his childhood, it was a high school teacher, whose intervention left a mark on him, who pulled him out of an adolescence that could have turned troubled. “Even if you’re not from the hood, moments of chaos are always there. They’re moments when you have the chance to take back control of your life,” he says.
Après avoir entrepris des études d’archi: After starting architecture studies, José turned, against all odds, to dance training. “When I started dancing, I didn’t see people like me. What if it’s actually me who has to do it? I felt it was something calling me – that I wanted to represent myself and put myself forward. It’s not always easy, but it was a motivation,” the dancer says.
S’il s’inspire beaucoup du vécu d’Eric V: Although it draws heavily on Eric Vega’s lived experience, the story of PAS FOUT’ MIND remains a work of fiction. There are still some very personal details, notably a conversation between the character and his father that he reproduced word for word. “Lots of immigrant parents and immigrant sons will see this and say: ‘Every day, we go through this!’” he exclaims amid laughter.
Comment la pièce a-t-elle été reçue par: How was the play received by those close to him? “It’s been very positive,” the actor confides. His father saw the play without his knowing. “He loved it, he cried, I heard things I’d rarely heard: I’m proud of you, it was really beautiful,” the actor recounts. He adds, laughing: “He’s also my landlord now; I feel like he’ll understand if I’m late paying my rent!” “I don’t invite my father to see the plays I do. He doesn’t understand, he falls asleep, he doesn’t care. That’s normal. It’s dark; people start speaking in alexandrines,” he adds, still with humour.
Son père est originaire du Honduras, et: His father is from Honduras, and his mother from El Salvador. Eric spent a formative period in his mother’s country as a teenager, a period he recounts in the play. Later, he obtained Salvadoran citizenship. “It’s complex, I grew up in Spanish with Salvadoran food, Latin American shows. When I get to school, I switch to a new culture: Quebec culture,” he says. “Even now, there are plenty of Quebec pop culture references that I don’t get.” He recounts, laughing, that at theatre school everyone exclaimed over a teacher who had been on a children’s show, and that he had to look on Google to find out who she was.
Au cours de la discussion qui suit l’une: During the discussion that follows one of the performances of PAS FOUT’ MIND, several audience members speak about the play. “I was a teacher for 20 years in Côte-des-Neiges and it made me think a lot of that, of immigrants’ kids. I’m Chilean myself. It’s a great source of pride for me to see you. It’s a very beautiful gift,” says one participant.
« En représentant le <em>hood</em> montr: “By representing the Montréal hood, you represent us too. We found ourselves in this play. It feels good to recognize yourself in theatre,” one hears. “We’ve all been through that in some way, and we’ve all had those encounters in life, we’ve had somewhat turbulent paths, it’s good to represent that in theatre,” says another participant.
Et comment le <em>hood</em> lui-même a-t: And how did the hood itself receive the play? “The hood came!” exclaims Eric Vega. He names the characters inspired by people he knew, who came to the show. “One of the dangerous places is social media. And it’s going well. Nobody’s trying to cancel me,” says the actor, laughing. He says, however, that the show’s good reception is the result of a lot of effort. “Yes, we’re lucky, but there’s work involved. We asked ourselves lots of questions about how to tell this story,” Eric continues, comparing the experience to walking a tightrope.
« C’est sensible parce qu’à Montréal, il: “It’s sensitive because in Montréal, there’s been a lot about this subject, about the violence found among young people these days. I imagine it’s hard for you to talk about it,” says another participant. “But I’ll suggest to the people around me, to all young people, to come see this play to see the brakes,” she says.
« Quand j’étais jeune, je ne voyais pas: “When I was young, I didn’t see Latino actors. My wish is that this has a life afterward, especially with young people, in the city, in Montréal,” says a young Latino actor who came to see PAS FOUT’ MIND. “Would you like to go into the neighbourhoods?” asks a community worker, who points out that spaces exist to stage such a show there.
Le producteur Xavier Inchauspé indique q: Producer Xavier Inchauspé says the play was designed to tour. So we can hope that Orange Noyée, the theatre company behind PAS FOUT’ MIND, will make sure the play makes its way to the hood.
« Bravo. Tu avais 17 ans, tu étais assis: “Bravo. You were 17, you were sitting in my math class, you were super straight, all put together, with your earphones in, doing your math exercises. I never could have imagined everything you told us earlier. I met you right when you’d just enlisted in the army,” says an audience member, who turns out to be a former teacher of Eric’s.
« Je vais revenir te voir, j’espère que: “I’ll come back to see you, and I hope Louis-Riel will come see you in large numbers. I’ll definitely spread the word,” she promises to close the discussion.
